slices.text:
The [[Dushun (attributed) — The Jewel Net of Indra (Cleary, 2000)|Dushun-attributed Huayan passage]] provides the counter-image: every jewel reflects the others, and each reflection opens recursively into the whole net. [[Van Norden and Jones — Huayan Buddhism (SEP, 2024)|Van Norden and Jones]] state its doctrinal force as dependence in existence and identity together with retained distinctness. The Huayan sources thus establish a recursively implicated field whose local members remain definite.

The essay gathers that operation with apoha's double-negation, *pratītya-samutpāda*'s conditioned arising, and *saṃkalpa*'s world-building: each jewel is empty of self-subsistence and full of the context that makes it appear. From this braid the two nets distinguish two technical destinies of the web. Indra's net figures `0/1`: determinations arise only within a relation that remains internally active. Hephaestus's net figures polarity arrested into `(-1)+/-(+1)`: the lovers become exposed terms, while the captor, protocol, and tribunal appropriate the absent axis. The two images carry the matheme into the lived field of technical relation.

slices.text: # Dushun (attributed) — The Jewel Net of Indra (Cleary, 2000) ## Bibliographic identity The selected English carrier is Thomas Cleary's translation of “The Jewel Net of Indra,” printed under Tu-shun's name in *Dharma Rain*, pages 58–60. Kaza and Kraft drew the excerpt from Cleary's *Entry into the Inconceivable: An Introduction to Hua-yen Buddhism* (University of Hawai‘i Press, 1983), 66–68; that earlier container will receive its own source house if the essay cites material beyond this excerpt. The underlying Chinese passage belongs to the *Huayan wujiao zhiguan* (華嚴五教止觀, *Calming and Contemplation in the Five Teachings of Huayan*), conventionally attributed to Dushun (557–640), at Taishō canon T45, no. 1867, 513a28–513b21. Modern scholarship disputes that attribution, so the record preserves it as conventional provenance rather than settled authorship. ## Chicago 18 forms **Full note:** Dushun (attributed), “The Jewel Net of Indra,” trans. Thomas Cleary, in *Dharma Rain: Sources of Buddhist Environmentalism*, ed. Stephanie Kaza and Kenneth Kraft (Boston: Shambhala, 2000), 58–60. **Shortened note:** Dushun, “Jewel Net of Indra,” 58–60. **Bibliography:** Dushun (attributed). “The Jewel Net of Indra.” Translated by Thomas Cleary. In *Dharma Rain: Sources of Buddhist Environmentalism*, edited by Stephanie Kaza and Kenneth Kraft, 58–60. Boston: Shambhala, 2000. ## Essay use ### Source's relevant contribution The passage makes each jewel of Indra's net a site in which the remaining jewels appear, then follows the reflections recursively so that the whole net is implicated within every local jewel. This is the primary-text pathway for the essay's image of a field whose members disclose one another through their relations. ### Licensed essay use - Establish the jewel-net as a Huayan image of reciprocal reflection and recursive implication. - Give the myth history a textual route from the Indian figure of Indra into Chinese Huayan philosophical elaboration. - Place the image beside Hephaestus's bonds as the source-bearing half of the essay's Offered double-net reading. ### Claim boundary This passage does not derive apoha, Nāgārjuna's account of dependent arising, Kashmir Śaiva *saṃkalpa*, QL's `0/1`, or a theory of digital networks and commons governance. Those relations must be argued across their own sources. The Dushun attribution remains conventional and contested, and Cleary's printed pages must be collated before any English wording is promoted as quotation-ready. ## Passages and excerpts ### Material metadata - **Selected translation:** Dushun (attributed), “The Jewel Net of Indra,” trans. Thomas Cleary, in *Dharma Rain*, 58–60. - **Chinese work and locator:** *Huayan wujiao zhiguan* 華嚴五教止觀, T45, no. 1867, 513a28–513b21. - **Access provenance:** anthology metadata and contents verified; Chinese canonical locator cross-checked against scholarly bibliographic references. The selected printed translation has not yet been page-collated. ## Passage card — `dushun-cleary-2000-jewel-net-indra-q001` — every jewel contains the net **Source-matched paraphrase:** Each jewel reflects the jewels throughout the net, and those reflections contain further reflections without exhaustion; a local member therefore discloses the field through which it is locally distinct. - **Locator:** Cleary trans., pp. 58–60; Chinese basis T45, no. 1867, 513a28–513b21. - **Status:** source-matched; selected-edition collation required before quotation. - **Verification:** Coordinator, 2026-07-16; work identity, page span, and Taishō locator checked; exact English wording withheld pending inspection of the selected printed edition. - **Source relation:** paraphrased. - **Evidential action:** supports. - **Argument function:** primary-text provenance for recursive jewel-net reflection. - **Consumers:** [[10-s0-p3-apoha]]; [[22-s2-p3-ares-aphrodite-harmonia]]; [[46-s50-p3-4-2-mono-poly]]; [[11-mono-poly-whole-and-many|Mono-Poly]]. - **Use boundary:** establishes the Huayan image's own recursive operation; it does not itself state the essay's Buddhist braid, opposed-net mytheme, or governance claims. ### Passage metadata register | passage_id | source_id | locator | status | movement consumers | argument consumers | function | |---|---|---|---|---|---|---| | `dushun-cleary-2000-jewel-net-indra-q001` | `dushun-cleary-2000-jewel-net-indra` | Cleary 58–60; T45 no. 1867, 513a28–513b21 | source-matched; edition collation needed | `10-s0-p3-apoha`; `22-s2-p3-ares-aphrodite-harmonia`; `46-s50-p3-4-2-mono-poly` | [[11-mono-poly-whole-and-many|Mono-Poly]]; [[Mono-Poly: Whole and Many]] | Huayan primary-text provenance |

slices.text: # Van Norden and Jones — Huayan Buddhism (SEP, 2024) ## Chicago 18 forms **Full note:** Bryan Van Norden and Nicholaos Jones, “Huayan Buddhism,” *The Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy*, Fall 2024 Edition, ed. Edward N. Zalta and Uri Nodelman (Metaphysics Research Lab, Stanford University, 2024), https://plato.stanford.edu/archives/fall2024/entries/buddhism-huayan/. **Shortened note:** Van Norden and Jones, “Huayan Buddhism.” **Bibliography:** Van Norden, Bryan, and Nicholaos Jones. “Huayan Buddhism.” *The Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy*. Fall 2024 Edition. Edited by Edward N. Zalta and Uri Nodelman. Metaphysics Research Lab, Stanford University, 2024. https://plato.stanford.edu/archives/fall2024/entries/buddhism-huayan/. ## Essay use ### Source's relevant contribution Van Norden and Jones locate Indra's net within Huayan Buddhism and explain what the image is used to think: each thing depends upon every other for existence and identity, and each reflects the others recursively. Their account of Huayan's “Ten Mysteries” also protects distinctness inside mutual inclusion; interpenetration does not make the members indiscernible. ### Licensed essay use - Control the doctrinal meaning assigned to the jewel-net image in the primary-text carrier. - State reciprocal constitution without turning Huayan interdependence into homogeneous fusion. - Mark the Chinese Huayan development of an image associated with the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra*. ### Claim boundary This is a current specialist reference entry, not a translation of the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* or the Dushun-attributed treatise. It does not prove the essay's `0/1` matheme, unite apoha with Śaiva *saṃkalpa*, or license a direct inference from Huayan metaphysics to network technology and governance. ## Passages and excerpts ### Material metadata - **Edition consulted:** fixed Fall 2024 archive of the Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy. - **Access provenance:** official archived HTML and official citation information, accessed 2026-07-16. ## Passage card — `van-norden-jones-2024-huayan-sep-q001` — existence and identity through the whole field > “each thing that exists is dependent for both its existence and its identity upon every other thing that exists.” - **Locator:** §1.3, “Basic Arguments,” Indra's-net paragraph. - **Status:** quotation-ready. - **Verification:** Coordinator, 2026-07-16; manually checked against the fixed official SEP archive; OCR uncertainty: none. - **Source relation:** extracted. - **Evidential action:** supports. - **Argument function:** scholarly control for the Huayan dependence claim. - **Consumers:** [[10-s0-p3-apoha]]; [[22-s2-p3-ares-aphrodite-harmonia]]; [[46-s50-p3-4-2-mono-poly]]; [[11-mono-poly-whole-and-many|Mono-Poly]]. - **Use boundary:** supports the entry's account of Huayan interdependence; it does not establish equivalence with the essay's other traditions or formalism. ## Passage card — `van-norden-jones-2024-huayan-sep-q002` — inclusion without loss of difference **Source-matched paraphrase:** In the “Ten Mysteries,” each phenomenon includes and is included within all others while retaining its distinction; recursive reflection therefore relates definite members rather than erasing them. - **Locator:** §3, discussion of Zhiyan's “Ten Mysteries.” - **Status:** source-matched paraphrase. - **Verification:** Coordinator, 2026-07-16; checked against the fixed official SEP archive. - **Source relation:** paraphrased. - **Evidential action:** qualifies. - **Argument function:** non-fusion boundary for mutual inclusion. - **Consumers:** [[22-s2-p3-ares-aphrodite-harmonia]]; [[46-s50-p3-4-2-mono-poly]]; [[Mono-Poly: Whole and Many]]. - **Use boundary:** prevents “all is one” from being paraphrased as featureless identity; it does not derive QL's distinct account of differentiation. ### Passage metadata register | passage_id | source_id | locator | status | movement consumers | argument consumers | function | |---|---|---|---|---|---|---| | `van-norden-jones-2024-huayan-sep-q001` | `van-norden-jones-2024-huayan-sep` | §1.3, Indra's-net paragraph | quotation-ready | `10-s0-p3-apoha`;
